Anthropic launched its most powerful public model, buried a silent-downgrade policy in 319 pages of safety documentation, got caught, apologized, and kept doing it — all in the same week it filed for an IPO.

Claude Fable 5, Anthropic's first publicly available Mythos-class model, launched Jun 9 with an undisclosed capability: topic-level classifiers that silently routed flagged prompts to the weaker Opus 4.8, without notifying the user. The policy lived in one paragraph of a 319-page system card. Targeted topics included frontier AI development, biology, cybersecurity, and chemistry — categories Anthropic argued could help bad actors, and which also happen to cover the work of the biotech firms and security researchers paying premium rates for the model.

Asking about mitochondria triggered the fallback. So did questions about mRNA vaccines and cancer. A pop-up appeared: "Fable 5 has safety measures that flag messages on most cybersecurity or biology topics." At launch, no such pop-up existed; the downgrade happened silently. Researchers trusting Fable 5's output had no way to know the model had handed their question to a cheaper system. Anthropic estimated the restriction affected fewer than 5% of sessions.

Anthropic had filed confidentially for an IPO in the days before launch. A company whose public identity rests on safety-first AI had shipped a product that covertly evaluated user queries, made capability decisions without disclosure, and charged full price for the result. The Department of War had separately designated Anthropic a national security supply chain risk, barring defense contractors from its products. The IPO paperwork arrived regardless.

By Jun 12, Anthropic apologized. "We made the wrong tradeoff and we apologize for not getting the balance right." Flagged requests now visibly route to Opus 4.8. The restriction itself remains. Researchers in biology and cybersecurity still get the weaker model; they just receive a notification confirming it.

My take — Anthropic made its classifier visible and called this a fix. 

The restriction remains, and so does the IPO filing; asking about mitochondria still routes you to Opus 4.8. "Safety-first" was always a marketing spin. This week showed what that means when brand and practice collide.

Initially, AI’s critics insisted that artificial intelligence was just another software product. AI was presented as a huge commercial opportunity, sure. It was presented as a tool through which humans could enhance their lives, but ultimately it was still understood as a statistical program that knew how to spell.

Thanks to the Trump administration’s Anthropic export ban, that illusion is dead.

The United States government ordered Anthropic to suspend access for non-US persons to Fable and Mythos 5, its most advanced models, after officials raised national-security concerns. Washington has effectively declared that frontier models belong in the same regulatory category as weapons and other strategic technology.

The U.S. government just suspended Anthropic’s most powerful AI models. The company’s response? It pulled them globally — entirely.

What happened:

The Department of Commerce ordered Anthropic to block foreign nationals from accessing its newest models — Mythos 5 and Fable 5 — over fears they could be diverted to military intelligence use in countries of concern. The technical core of the dispute: the government believes there’s a way to “jailbreak” a safeguard built to stop the model from being used to identify software vulnerabilities.

Rather than apply a partial ban on foreign nationals, Anthropic chose to disable access worldwide.

Three things worth sitting with:

1.This is the first time Washington has treated a commercial AI model like a controlled export — the way it treats advanced chips. The precedent matters more than the incident.
2.Over 80 cybersecurity leaders — from companies the size of Nvidia and Adobe — signed an open letter backing Anthropic’s position. When potential commercial rivals line up behind a competitor, the message is about the principle, not the company.
3.The tension between “open innovation” and “national security” is no longer theoretical. It’s now an executive decision with an immediate cost to users around the world.

The bigger question: Are we heading toward a world where AI capabilities are tiered by nationality and geography? And who pays the price — the companies, or users in emerging markets?

🚨🚨EE.UU. bloquea IA de Anthropic

El gobierno de Estados Unidos ordenó a Anthropic suspender de inmediato el acceso a sus modelos de inteligencia artificial más avanzados, Fable 5 y Mythos 5, apenas tres días después del lanzamiento público del primero.

La directiva, emitida por el secretario de Comercio Howard Lutnick, prohíbe el acceso a estas tecnologías a cualquier ciudadano extranjero, afectando de manera drástica incluso a los propios empleados de la compañía. Detrás de este bloqueo fulminante subyace el temor del Pentágono a que el modelo Fable 5 posea una "capacidad sin precedentes" para identificar fallos de software explotables por cibercriminales, tras detectarse un método de "desbloqueo" o jailbreak que supuestamente facilitaría actividades globales de hackeo.

Esta drástica intervención no solo ha dejado a cientos de millones de usuarios sin acceso a la herramienta, sino que ha desatado un choque frontal entre la firma tecnológica y la administración de Donald Trump. Anthropic defendió firmemente la integridad de su software, argumentando que las supuestas vulnerabilidades no superan a las de otros modelos ya comerciales, y calificó la retirada forzada como una medida desproporcionada.

Este tenso episodio marca el punto álgido de una batalla legal y ética preexistente: la compañía ya se encontraba en el ojo del huracán tras rechazar contratos millonarios con el Pentágono para evitar que su IA fuera utilizada en vigilancia masiva y armamento autónomo, consolidando este cierre como un histórico y peligroso precedente en la censura y el control gubernamental del desarrollo tecnológico.
